title: Pan pipes
reference_instrument: an Andean siku, for family likeness and with no count: the nearest isolated tube by pitch from the Wikimedia Commons set Registro sonoro del Siku (D3 from Bajo Sanja - Arca, G3 and D4 from Sanja - Ira, B4 from Contra Suli - Arca; Abel Christian Apaza Amanqui, Sikuri Sumaq Taqi, CC BY-SA 4.0). A siku is a different instrument from the modelled stopped pipes and is not tuned to A440
summary: Andean pan pipes assembled from published rules, not from a measured instrument: the note set of a zampona (G major), the tube bore scaling of measured panpipes and the lip-jet controls of a player (Fletcher 2005, with the blowing pressure and jet length at each pitch from the flute-player relations of Fletcher 1975), with each tube's length computed from its note and blown one tube at a time as a stopped pipe filled with the gas Coltman measured in a played flute's bore. Speaks; not graded on the site. Screened siku recordings now exist (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0, 26 pitches), and each note's page now sets one beside its render with no count, but the grader has no library for them yet; G4 and B4 were measured against them with the grader's own functions only (see what is missing). No published table of measured siku or zampona tube lengths could be reached, and nothing here claims to match a real instrument.
physics_present: fs-couple flue_loop: a lip jet acting on a stopped cylindrical tube, with its blowing pressure and jet length at each tube's equal-tempered pitch from Fletcher 1975's measured flute-player relations (p [mbar] = 0.008 nu, l [mm] = 1.8 + 100 nu^(-1/2); 117.5 Pa and 10.05 mm at D3 to 395.1 Pa and 6.30 mm at B4) and its lip height from the published range ends, 1 mm to 0.5 mm, paired linearly in log2 f
the stopped-pipe resonator: closed at the far end, open at the blown top, with the published bore scaling and the open-end correction

the published stopped-pipe jet offset: the closed end blocks the steady flow so the jet passes outside the lip by about half a jet half-width (Fletcher 2005 Eqs. 4 to 6, 0.5 b), applied as the labium offset: the committed cards put it at 0.25 flue heights, half the half-width at the flue; the posted cards at half the half-width the jet has spread to at the lip (offset/b 0.50: 1.086, 0.962, 0.803 and 0.618 mm at D3, G3, D4 and B4)

the posted cards (pan-pipes-<note>-forced-jet-spreading-half-width-offset-re700, D3 G3 D4 B4; ledger pan-pipes-wlh-posted-cards) are the committed card plus: the forced Bickley jet with the momentum drive at weight 1 (Thwaites and Fletcher 1983 Eq. 1, as printed), Fletcher 1976's jet spreading law as a TRIAL (his flues were 0.25 to 1.0 mm high, these are 1.00 to 2.00 mm), Verge 1995's flue-jet noise fraction at onset Re_h 700 carried to these flues as an extrapolation, the recorder mouth's contraction loss (Auvray 2014) carried to a stopped pipe, the computed baffled radiation and the Stokes-Kirchhoff observer gas. Rendered on ts1 on 2026-11-04 (hold 1.0 to 2.0 s of 2.5 s) they speak the named note in the first register, 4.5, 7.3, 11.7 and 17.8 cents flat of the tempered design (D3, G3, D4, B4), with the third harmonic level with the first (H3 re H1 -2.7, -1.7, -0.8 and -0.5 dB) and the second harmonic at -60.7, -62.5, -65.1 and -66.3 dB
fractional-delay propagation and gas-derived viscothermal loss along the tube

radiation observed at a physical receiver 1 m above the open top (the committed cards: the compact baffled load; the posted cards: the computed baffled radiation with the compact baffled reaction at the mouth, receiver band 1185, 1342, 1597 and 1989 Hz at D3, G3, D4 and B4)

the tubes' gas: the gas Coltman measured in a played flute's bore (Physics Today 21(11), 1968, p. 27; ledger coltman-1968-flute-bore-gas), as the three flute cards carry it: the explicit mixture at 26.15 C (299.30 K), 101325 Pa, saturated, 2.5 percent dry CO2 and 18.5 percent dry O2, with the observer and radiation exterior kept as dry air at 20 C. It is a measurement of a flute bore applied to stopped pipes by analogy, not of a played pan pipe, and a stopped tube may exchange far less breath, so the real fill may lie closer to room air: the bracket runs from dry 20 C air to this state (unknowns u-bore-gas). Measured with the card controls of u-player-controls, on one binary, it raises every tube by 16.6 to 16.7 cents over dry 20 C air and by 5.4 to 5.5 cents over the shared woodwind pack the cards carried before (27 C, 4.5 percent dry CO2); the level and the grader's envelope, harmonic and combined spectral distances to a recording move by no more than 0.1 dB, and the render's HNR stays at the solver's numerical floor (79 dB) because it has no noise

the player's jet controls are a law measured on flute players, applied to a stopped pipe by analogy, as Fletcher 2005 does for the jet speed: neither paper measures a pan-pipe player, D3 lies below every pitch the source reports and G3 is the alto flute's lowest note, covered by an unplotted sentence. Against the previous controls (the range ends paired linearly in log2 f) the pressure is 0.40 to 0.49 of theirs and the jet length 1 to 26 percent longer; every note still speaks its first register under the card's jet, 13 to 18 cents flatter and 7 to 10 dB quieter. Against the sikus (G4 and B4) the grader's combined spectral distance falls by 0.5 to 2.2 dB and the centroid ratio by about a quarter, and the render is still 2.3 to 5.2 times too bright. Under the forced Bickley jet without the momentum drive these controls sound the third register on D3, G3 and D4 (a twelfth above the named note); the posted cards keep the momentum drive on and speak the first register on all four, but at the 20 m/s jet speed Fletcher 2005 prints, D3 and G3 with the momentum drive on jump to the third mode, so the controls do not decide the register (unknowns u-player-controls)
a self-sustained oscillation: each tube settles to a steady tone and re-rendering with another jet seed gives the same pitch and level
physics_missing: a graded comparison: screened siku recordings exist (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0, 26 pitches, 44 valid clips), but the grader's library is built from UIowa-named files and holds none of them, so no pair is graded; the site plays each posted note beside one real siku tube, the nearest of 94 by pitch, with no count. Measured directly with the grader's own functions (instrgrade-4, no real-vs-real ruler), G4 against three sikus and B4 against one, the renders sit far from the recordings: spectral centroid 2.3 to 5.2 times too high, upper-harmonic share 9 to 21 dB too high, and an HNR of 79 dB against the recordings' 9 to 22 dB, because the render has no breath noise. No claim of resemblance is made

measured tube lengths and bores of a real siku or zampona: the lengths are computed from the notes and the bore from a regression on European panpipes. Andean tubes are much less regular, so this is a design from published rules, not a model of an instrument

the even harmonics of the posted cards: with the offset at half the spread half-width the cut flow carries H2 re H1 of -16.4, -17.9, -20.1 and -23.3 dB (D3, G3, D4, B4; the tanh cut of Fletcher and Douglas 1980, swing A/b 2.54, 2.85, 3.29 and 4.06), but the radiated H2 is -60.7, -62.5, -65.1 and -66.3 dB because the stopped pipe blocks 2f: the mouth flow's 2f line sits 47.4, 48.0, 42.9 and 43.5 dB under the cut flow's. The committed cards (offset 0.25 flue heights, no forced jet) sound odd harmonics only. See the open-gap line below

even harmonics against real tubes, an open gap and not a claim: the screened siku clips (Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0, 94 isolated tubes of 14 studio files) read H2 re H1 at a median of -17.0 dB (quartiles -22.5 to -12.4, H3 -9.8 dB), where the chain printed in Fletcher 2005 (the jet's flow into the pipe from Fletcher and Douglas 1980, then the stopped pipe's flow response, Eqs. 7 and 8) gives about -68 to -83 dB for the cards' tubes (D3 to B4, with the cut-flow line read from the renders) and the posted renders give -61 to -66 dB. No printed source separates non-ideal pipe walls or tuning, a larger jet offset at high notes, or anything else as the cause of the difference, so the cause is recorded as unknown (unknowns u-even-harmonic-gap)

pitch of the committed cards (no forced jet): with the flute's bore gas in the tubes and the flute-player controls the notes land 17.5 to 23.5 cents flat of the tempered design (D3 -17.5, G3 -18.5, D4 -18.5, G4 -18.9, B4 -23.5; with the shared woodwind pack -22.9 to -29.0 and with dry air -34.1 to -40.2; with the previous controls -8.6 to -11.3 with the pack and -19.6 to -22.3 with dry air, the jet pulling the pitch further flat at the lower pressure). The passive pipe is already 10.6 to 11.8 cents flat of the design table with this gas (D3 -10.6, G3 -10.8, D4 -11.2, G4 -11.5, B4 -11.8; computed from the card's network with the first-order wide-tube wall layer and the flue island's mouth inertance, a model that returns the design to 0.01 cents when given the cutting rule's own mouth and no wall layer): the tube lengths were cut for dry 20 C air with L = c/(4 f) - 0.6133 a (unknowns u-tube-lengths), a rule with no boundary-layer phase-speed term, and the wall layer of the card's own loss law lowers the speed in these bores by 1.2 to 1.3 percent. Rendered with that law switched off, every tube rises 20.7 to 22.1 cents (D3 +21.9, G3 +21.9, D4 +21.2, G4 +20.7, B4 +22.1) against 20.5 to 22.5 computed, so the wall layer is the largest term. The flue island's mouth end correction, 0.61 times the equivalent radius of the flue opening, is 0.8 to 1.6 millimetres longer in bore length than the thin-wall value the tubes were cut for and lowers them by 4.7 to 7.9 cents; the gas brings 16.3 cents back (16.6 to 16.7 rendered). The jet then adds 7 to 12 cents flat at these controls (7 to 10 with the loss law off) and pulled 6 to 8 cents sharp at the previous ones, so its pull depends on the player controls. The note set is the theoretical equal-tempered table at A=440 (design frequencies of Sanchez Barrero and Ghezzi 2010), not a tuned instrument, and the lengths are left as cut. Real sikus are not tuned to equal temperament either: the three G4 recordings measure -12.2, -29.1 and -28.4 cents and the one B4 recording +36.7 cents of the tempered note, so the mean distance of the G4 render from them is 8.8 cents (7.0 with the shared pack, 8.1 with dry air and the previous controls, 13.2 with the pack and the previous controls) and of the B4 render 60.2 cents (65.7 with the shared pack, 59.0 and 48.0 with the previous controls)

pitch of the posted cards: -4.5, -7.3, -11.7 and -17.8 cents of the tempered design at D3, G3, D4 and B4 (ts1 renders, hold 1.0 to 2.0 s); the split into passive pipe, gas, wall layer, mouth correction and jet pull above was measured on the committed cards and is not repeated for these

the jet: the card is an estimate for a lip jet, not a measured jet card, and the jet is only 5.0 to 6.3 times its height (5.03 at D3, 5.08 G3, 5.34 D4, 5.76 G4, 6.30 B4), under the 5.6 where the island's phase correction is exact for D3, G3 and D4 and over it for G4 and B4; the displacement gain is the demonstrator value, the lip aperture width is taken as the tube width, and the jet spreading across the top of the tube is not modelled on the committed cards (the posted cards apply Fletcher 1976's law as a trial outside its measured range)
the percussive Andean playing style with a turbulent jet; only the normal laminar style is rendered
neighbouring tubes: they are not coupled, nor is the array radiation or the player's lips and face

onset ramp, mouth loss and breath noise: authored, neutral or absent on the committed cards; the posted cards carry the recorder mouth's contraction loss and Verge's flue-jet noise as extrapolations, not pan-pipe measurements (the bore's gas is Coltman 1968's played-flute state, unknowns u-bore-gas)
a radiating outlet at the closed end: the generic input needs one radiating outlet, so a tiny vent of a vanishing fraction of the bore area stands in for it
native verification beyond a single clock and two jet seeds on two notes
